title: Scooby-Doo's name from Sinatra
hook: A cartoon dog was named after Frank Sinatra's scat at the end of a love song.
peek: Scooby-Doo was nearly a bongo-playing dog called Too Much. A television executive renamed him after hearing Frank Sinatra sing "scooby dooby doo" at the end of Strangers in the Night, and the name stuck in 1969.
lede: In 1969 the Hanna-Barbera studio was developing a cartoon about teenagers who solve mysteries with their dog. The CBS executive Fred Silverman has said that on a flight he heard Frank Sinatra's Strangers in the Night, which ends with Sinatra crooning "scooby dooby doo". He decided the dog should be called Scooby-Doo, and the show became Scooby-Doo, Where Are You.

bullets.text: Early pitches were called Mysteries Five, about a teenage band, with a bongo-playing dog named Too Much. The band idea was dropped, the cast shrank to four and the dog became the star once he had a better name.

Sinatra's song came out in 1966, topped the charts and won Grammy awards. His relaxed scat at the fade-out was an ad lib, not part of the written lyric, which makes it an unlikely source for a famous name.

The designer Iwao Takamoto talked to a Great Dane breeder about what makes a prize dog, then did the opposite for Scooby: a sloping back, bowed legs and a small chin. The awkward shape suited a cowardly cartoon dog.
Don Messick voiced Scooby for about 25 years, giving him the famous growly way of talking that adds an R to words. The catchphrase "Scooby dooby doo" brought the dog's name back round to Sinatra.
